title: Inhabitant: An Agent Framework for Long-Horizon Human-Scene Interaction with Spatial Control and Quantitative Feedback
why: A-type training-free language-model agent harness for long-horizon human-scene interaction: the agent specifies motions by positions, paths and poses, measures how the executed interaction deviates from its intent, and revises the control specification, with a new Inhabit benchmark of household whole-body tasks.
mechanism: A language-model agent plans and executes a sequence of interactions in a 3D scene under one instruction. Inhabitant is training-free: the agent specifies each motion through positions, paths and poses, measures deviation of the executed interaction from that intent, and revises the control specification. The authors also introduce Inhabit, a benchmark of 75 household tasks in 31 furniture layouts, each chaining one to three goals on movable objects and carried out by the whole body, excluding fingers.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): on Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7% of the tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, and 93.3% and 82.7% with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, respectively. Ablations are reported to confirm that without spatial control the agent fails most tasks, and without quantitative feedback its motion becomes less precise. Numeric tables unread.

title: Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks
why: B-type evaluation-methodology paper (SimAudit): an LLM-based pipeline that audits hand-written success checkers on simulated manipulation benchmarks for phantom successes and silent failures, directly relevant to how closed-loop success is judged.
mechanism: SimAudit is an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions. It analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify disagreement scenarios, recreates those scenarios in simulation, runs the original checker, and uses multi-view renderings to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction. The authors distinguish phantom success (accepting an incomplete execution) from silent failure (rejecting an execution that satisfies the instruction).
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict. Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures. Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0. Numeric tables unread.

title: Bridging vision-language reasoning and learned control for legged navigation in the wild
why: A-type hierarchical harness (ROAM) that couples a pre-trained VLM’s scene reasoning, risk assessment and sign interpretation with open-vocabulary segmentation and two frozen RL policies for locomotion and local navigation on a legged robot in real alpine and urban settings.
mechanism: ROAM combines a Vision-Language Model pre-trained on internet-scale data with locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via RL. The VLM assesses risks, interprets signs, and produces semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts those labels into a dense real-time risk map that conditions two pre-trained RL policies for agile locomotion and local navigation.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): real-world experiments in complex alpine and urban settings; the robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and identifies safe areas on which to step. The authors also note remaining challenges in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning. Trial counts and numeric tables are not stated in the abstract.

title: Verify2Act: Critic-Guided Latent World Models for Verifying Language-Conditioned Manipulation Plans
why: A-type pre-execution verification harness: a VLM proposes multi-step manipulation plans, a latent world model imagines them, and a dual-head critic checks temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before anything is executed on a robot arm.
mechanism: Verify2Act separates semantic action proposal from latent physical verification. A VLM proposes candidate plans; a latent world model (V2A-WM) imagines each plan in DINOv2 feature space; a dual-head critic checks the imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before execution. V2A-WM extends flow-matching world models with cross-attention action grounding and a causal temporal history window. The world model and critic are trained only on data generated in a digital twin and the full system is deployed on a low-cost robot arm.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): across six language-conditioned tasks, Verify2Act reaches 83.3% task success, compared with 61.7% for a latent world model without the authors’ architectural changes, 53.3% for the VLM alone, and 46.7% for a pixel-diffusion world model. The authors state it verified every plan it executed and incurred no planning-induced failures; failed episodes were caused by low-level grasp or placement slips. In simulation, they report the highest five-task chain success on CALVIN among compared baselines with 30× fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification, and the highest success on cluttered nut assembly. Numeric tables and trial counts unread.

title: CoachSI: Self-Improvement of Robot Policies with a Language Coach
why: A-type teacher-harness self-improvement: a frozen off-the-shelf VLM coaches a robot policy in language by naming the next atomic step (never outputting an action); successful coached rollouts are relabeled and used to fine-tune the policy, which is then deployed unassisted.
mechanism: CoachSI uses a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model as a language coach. The VLM watches the robot and names the next step in the format of the policy’s atomic instructions, and never outputs an action. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction and used to fine-tune the policy. The fine-tuned policy is then deployed on its own. The authors state that the gain is obtained with the action backbone frozen.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): on states where a World Action Model and a Vision-Language-Action model have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6× over the unchanged task instruction. After fine-tuning, unassisted success on long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8%, above both baselines. Numeric tables unread.

title: A²-VLA: Adapting Vision-Language-Action Policies to New Tools through Agentic Affordance Discovery
why: A-type tool-adaptation harness around a VLA: an embodied agent constructs, tests and revises tool-affordance hypotheses, accumulates validated extraction skills in a reusable library, and conditions a π0.5 backbone on functional-region features for unseen tools.
mechanism: A²-VLA combines an embodied agent with a VLA policy and treats tool affordances as hypotheses the agent can construct, test, and revise. Given teleoperated demonstrations with a few source tools, the agent reconstructs the scenes in simulation, autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features (functional regions and key geometric properties), develops affordance-extraction skills, and refines both features and skills through autonomous experiments. Validated extraction skills accumulate in a reusable skill library for unseen tools. Encoded functional-region features then condition a π0.5 backbone at training and inference.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): evaluation examines affordance reliability in reconstructed scenes and real-robot task success on unseen tools. The method achieves 86.1% success in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting based on affordances. On three real-robot tool-use tasks, A²-VLA improves task success by 30.7 percentage points over π0.5. Numeric tables and trial counts unread.

title: EmbodyAgent: Post-Training Embodied VLM Agents via Distillation, SFT, and RL
why: A-type post-training stack that turns an open-weight VLM into a code-as-policy robot-use agent via black-box teacher distillation, SFT, and online RL, all sharing one primitive-free Python execution tool over raw visual observation and seven-dimensional end-effector control.
mechanism: EmbodyAgent has three coupled pipelines: (1) a black-box data synthesis pipeline that queries a strong teacher under a forced think-then-code contract and filters trajectories by task success; (2) an SFT pipeline that distills explanation-and-program targets into an open-weight 9B VLM with both vision and language encoders trainable; and (3) an online RL pipeline that optimizes student-generated episodes via group-relative advantage with a runtime-error-penalized outcome reward. All three pipelines share one primitive-free Python execution tool exposing only raw visual observation and seven-dimensional end-effector control, with no action decoder and no interface shift across stages. The authors also describe a self-reinforcing runtime-error mode induced by outcome-based RL on executable code, and a failure-category monitoring and sampling-side curation protocol.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): under a strictly separated evaluation protocol on ten LIBERO Spatial tasks (disjoint state splits, greedy test-time decoding, training-only safeguards), held-out success on 100 test states rises from 0/100 (base 9B VLM) to 14/100 (after SFT) and 84/100 (after RL), while training rollout success climbs from 8.4% to 87.7% and median model calls per episode drop from 36 to 11. Numeric tables unread.

title: Reasoning on Call: Efficient Agentic Robot Control for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
why: A-type execution-control harness (RoC) that coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor, triggering agent review only when needed for execution repair and plan revision in long-horizon manipulation.
mechanism: RoC (Reasoning on Call) coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor combines temporal visual observations with ordered interaction memory to estimate progress within the active subtask and predict its successor. Those predictions guide event-triggered agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions, so routine execution stays with the policy while reasoning focuses on decisions that need additional assessment.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): on RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3% compared with the strongest agent-based baseline, and outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Real-world experiments are reported across three long-horizon manipulation tasks. Numeric tables and trial counts unread.

title: Alignment Drives Reuse: Learning Generalizable Robot-Use Agents from Heterogeneous Experience
why: A-type robot-use-agent framework (UniCraft) that aligns geometry, sensing and control interfaces across embodiments and benchmarks so interaction feedback can jointly refine a shared skillset and an orchestration policy, without demonstrations or weight updates.
mechanism: UniCraft represents observed scene geometry with consistent coordinate conventions and aligns sensing and control interfaces across robots. It organizes tasks from different benchmarks in a canonical format, allowing interaction feedback to jointly refine shared skills and the orchestration policy that guides their selection and composition, without any demonstrations or model weight updates. The authors interleave tasks from 3 benchmarks and 6 embodiments, collecting 2,700 learning rollouts per agent model. After training, the learned skills are frozen for zero-shot transfer.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): during training, UniCraft improves pooled task success on unseen scenarios and tasks by 9-28 percentage points on LIBERO-PRO, 10.8-13.3 on RoboTwin 2.0, and 3.1-14.4 on RoboCasa365 (Epochs 1-3). After training, with the learned skills frozen, UniCraft demonstrates zero-shot transfer across 4 new robot embodiments and 5 additional agent models on robosuite and RoboDojo. Numeric tables unread.

title: ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain
why: A-type slow-fast VLN harness that gives a frozen (no navigation-domain SFT) VLM brain a semantic tool-calling interface in natural language to an action expert, then jointly improves both through closed-loop agentic RL.
mechanism: ZeroVLN is a slow-fast navigation framework that does no navigation-domain supervised fine-tuning of the VLM brain. Instead of teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, it equips the brain with a semantic tool-calling interface that conveys movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. The action expert is first adapted to carry out those movement requests; then the brain’s movement decisions and the action expert’s continuous execution are jointly improved through closed-loop reinforcement learning. The authors report only minor changes to the brain’s weights and that general visual capabilities are largely preserved.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain’s weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. The authors claim it is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE. Numeric tables unread.

title: JARVIS: An Agent That Designs, Builds, and Tests Circuit Boards on Its Own
why: A-type embodied coding-agent harness that closes a physical design–build–test–learn loop for circuit boards: a robot arm, PCB printer and pick-and-place machine are coordinated from a text instruction, with digital-twin rehearsal, sensor verification, measurement-based diagnosis, and redesign.
mechanism: JARVIS is an embodied agent for circuit-board development. It maintains machine-specific capabilities and constraints, scans its workspace with a robot-mounted 3D scanner, and constructs an executable digital twin in which it rehearses robot motions, fabrication steps, and circuit behavior before consuming materials. A single text instruction initiates the physical experiment. Using unmodified desktop equipment, the agent coordinates a robot arm, a PCB printer that deposits conductive silver ink and solder paste, and a pick-and-place machine. It verifies progress with cameras and sensors, tests the fabricated circuit with an OPAL-RT real-time simulator and an oscilloscope, diagnoses deviations from the design, and generates a revised design in KiCad for subsequent rehearsal.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): in a demonstration involving a 60 Hz notch filter for grid-connected converter sensing, JARVIS completed a first-run experiment in 2 h 39 min without human intervention, achieving 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz. Its digital-twin rehearsal identified five issues before fabrication, including a test criterion that would have incorrectly rejected a functioning board. During execution, the agent also resolved encountered faults autonomously. Numeric tables unread.

title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
why: B-type evaluation-methodology paper: an intent-grounded critique framework and action-level analysis of frontier multimodal agents that command robots via low-level numerical actions, plus a human-annotated critic benchmark and a released action dataset.
mechanism: AgentRoboCritic is an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action’s outcome and failure mode against this intent. The authors use it for a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. They also validate the critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): action-level analysis is said to show closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation, as well as limitations in physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. The fine-tuned critic’s failure-mode accuracy is reported to rise from 32.58% to 74.24%. Numeric tables unread.
